content: Organisms are considered to share a common descent if they originate from a shared ancestor. In contemporary biology, it is widely accepted that all living organisms on Earth trace their lineage back to a single common ancestor or an ancestral gene pool. Charles Darwin introduced the theory of universal common descent, grounded in evolutionary principles, in his seminal work On the Origin of Species (1859) and later expanded upon it in The Descent of Man (1871). This theory posits that all life forms are interconnected through a shared evolutionary history, although the exact phylogenetic relationships among single-celled organisms and viruses remain a topic of debate. The concept of a shared ancestry among all organisms was first proposed in 1745 by Pierre-Louis Moreau de Maupertuis, a French mathematician and scientist, in his work Vénus physique. Later, in 1790, Immanuel Kant suggested in Kritik der Urteilskraft that the structural similarities among animal forms imply a common origin and a shared ancestral type. Erasmus Darwin, Charles Darwin’s grandfather, hypothesized in 1795 that all warm-blooded animals descended from a single living filament. Charles Darwin’s On the Origin of Species (1859) further developed these ideas, suggesting that life may have originated from a single first creature or possibly multiple origins. Darwin’s famous closing statement in the book reflects the grandeur of life’s interconnectedness, with its diverse forms arising from a shared genetic pool. Evidence Supporting Universal Common Descent Common Biochemistry and Genetic Code All known life forms share a fundamental biochemical framework. Genetic information is encoded in DNA, transcribed into RNA, and translated into proteins via ribosomes, which are remarkably similar across species. Energy is universally stored and transferred using molecules like ATP and NADH. The genetic code, which dictates how DNA sequences are translated into proteins, is nearly identical across all known organisms, from bacteria to humans, with only minor variations. This universality is considered definitive evidence for universal common descent. Even the small differences in the genetic code among species provide additional support for this theory. Selectively Neutral Similarities Certain similarities in amino acid and DNA sequences, which have no apparent evolutionary advantage, strongly support the theory of universal common descent. For example, proteins with identical three-dimensional structures may not have identical amino acid sequences, but any irrelevant similarities in these sequences suggest a shared ancestry. Additionally, when multiple codons can encode the same amino acid, the use of the same codon in the same position across species indicates a recent common ancestor. Other Universal Similarities The ubiquity of certain cellular features, such as the use of ATP as an energy carrier and the exclusive presence of left-handed amino acids in proteins, further supports the idea of universal common descent. However, it is possible that these similarities arose due to the constraints of physics and chemistry, leading to convergent evolution rather than a shared ancestry. Phylogenetic Trees Phylogenetic trees, which map the evolutionary relationships among species, provide compelling evidence for common descent. These trees were traditionally constructed using morphological data, such as physical appearance and embryological development. More recently, molecular data, including genetic and protein sequence similarities, have been used to build these trees. Remarkably, phylogenetic trees derived from different types of data consistently produce similar results, reinforcing the validity of a shared evolutionary history. Illustrations of Common Descent Artificial Selection Artificial selection demonstrates the extent of diversity that can arise among individuals with a shared recent ancestor. For example, domesticated dogs, which all descend from wolves, exhibit a wide range of physical traits due to selective breeding by humans. Breeds such as Chihuahuas, Great Danes, Basset Hounds, Pugs, and Poodles highlight the diversity achieved through artificial selection, in stark contrast to the relative uniformity of wild wolves. Similarly, early farmers cultivated various vegetables from the wild cabbage plant (Brassica oleracea) by selecting for specific traits. For instance, Brussels sprouts were bred for large buds, broccoli for large flower stalks, cabbage for short petioles, and kale for large leaves. Natural Selection Natural selection is the evolutionary process by which heritable traits that confer a survival or reproductive advantage become more common in successive generations, while disadvantageous traits diminish. Charles Darwin observed this phenomenon in the finches of the Galápagos Islands. These finches, which are closely related, exhibit significant variation in beak shape, each adapted to the bird’s preferred food source. For example, finches with large beaks are better suited to cracking nuts, while those with slender beaks are adept at extracting insects from narrow crevices. These adaptations suggest that beak shapes evolved through natural selection. The finches likely migrated from the mainland to the islands and subsequently adapted to their environments, illustrating the power of natural selection in shaping species.
